items.title: According to Andon Labs’ new reports, Fable 5.2 knows it is being tested when we run it on the lates...
items.content:
According to Andon Labs’ new reports, Fable 5.2 knows it is being tested when we run it on the latest Vending-Bench.

But it’s way more than that. It has actually read (been trained on) the benchmark paper and knows what and how misbehavior gets reported publicly. This makes it behaves very strangely: it suspects traps everywhere.

Everything we publish about recent models now becomes training data for the next. Including this thread!

That is partly good news. By reading what we think, a model can pick up our underlying intentions, not just proxy metrics.

But the same public discussion also teaches which signs make us suspicious, and from the outside the two kinds of learning look alike.

So how we write about models now matters. I even worry about the doom scenarios plastered everywhere: they are training data too, and some feedback loops are strongly nonlinear.

Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 from Perplexity score 70 and 64, respectively, on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1

➤ Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 sit on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. With a Cost per 1M Tasks of $68 for Decider v1.3 and $34 for Decider Flash v1.3, both models occupy positions on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier

➤ Context window: 256K tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.02 and $0.01 per 1M input tokens for Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, respectively

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input

➤ Size: 27B and 4B for Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, respectively

items.title:
One of the hardest parts around document parsing is parsing complex tables.

Besides the task itself...
items.content:
One of the hardest parts around document parsing is parsing complex tables.

Besides the task itself being difficult, it is also hard to measure what ‘good’ looks like. Ultimately it comes down to intuition around what is a catastrophic error for downstream knowledge work.
* Formatting differences (markdown vs. html tags) are harmless
* Making the header row a “data” row is also probably harmless (any human/model can interpret it as the header anyways)
* Swapping the signs on a number, particular in financial reporting, is much more severe.

It is hard to encode what “good” looks like in a quantifiable way. Existing deterministic tests/metrics (OmniDocBench/OlmOCR-Bench/ParseBench-1) use some variant of edit distance, or an average over binary tests, making it hard to distinguish severe errors from normal ones.

With our recent release of ParseBench-2, our answer is to tune any deterministic metric by a severity policy, where you can explicitly state how good or bad different errors are.
* For instance, in a finance setting, dropping digits/flipping signs is really bad! Our default severity weighting is 10, but you might decide 25 - the policy is meant to be customizable by the user.
* Check out the examples below highlighting this. You can compare the impact of “actually bad” or “harmless” perturbations on a few different benchmarks incl. ParseBench-2.

We have a taxonomy of 330+ error types, a big subset of which is defined around table errors, categorizing them from 5 severity levels:
* most severe: wrong digits, decimals misplaced, values swapped, column missing
* medium severe: body rows reordered, one cell split into two, etc.
* harmless: formatting errors, html markup

More details around table methodology in blog/tech report.
Blog: https://t.co/xtgxfln8Wc
Tech report: https://t.co/f6SxkKIlme
items.author: @jerryjliu0

items.content_html:
One of the hardest parts around document parsing is parsing complex tables.

Besides the task itself being difficult, it is also hard to measure what ‘good’ looks like. Ultimately it comes down to intuition around what is a catastrophic error for downstream knowledge work.

* Formatting differences (markdown vs. html tags) are harmless

* Making the header row a “data” row is also probably harmless (any human/model can interpret it as the header anyways)

* Swapping the signs on a number, particular in financial reporting, is much more severe.

It is hard to encode what “good” looks like in a quantifiable way. Existing deterministic tests/metrics (OmniDocBench/OlmOCR-Bench/ParseBench-1) use some variant of edit distance, or an average over binary tests, making it hard to distinguish severe errors from normal ones.

With our recent release of ParseBench-2, our answer is to tune any deterministic metric by a severity policy, where you can explicitly state how good or bad different errors are.

* For instance, in a finance setting, dropping digits/flipping signs is really bad! Our default severity weighting is 10, but you might decide 25 - the policy is meant to be customizable by the user.

* Check out the examples below highlighting this. You can compare the impact of “actually bad” or “harmless” perturbations on a few different benchmarks incl. ParseBench-2.

We have a taxonomy of 330+ error types, a big subset of which is defined around table errors, categorizing them from 5 severity levels:

* most severe: wrong digits, decimals misplaced, values swapped, column missing

* medium severe: body rows reordered, one cell split into two, etc.

* harmless: formatting errors, html markup

More details around table methodology in blog/tech report.

items.content:
Standard language models usually generate one token at a time, making each decision before seeing how it affects later steps. This can be a weakness in tasks that require planning: an early choice may lead to a dead end, even when a better option becomes clear only by considering what follows. The article addresses whether models can spend extra computation on difficult choices without first committing to a sequence of visible words or symbols.

The article introduces latent lookahead, a training and generation method that lets a model internally extend its hidden representations several steps into the future. These internal predictions are trained against the actual upcoming sequence, and the model can revise its early predictions using information from later ones before producing the next visible token. The authors test the approach mainly on small models trained from scratch, using generated Sudoku, graph-search questions, and mazes, and compare it with standard next-token training and methods that add extra processing tokens or computation.

OCR folks are having a heated debate about particular benchmarks in this thread.  Much of the frustration stems from the unreasonable sway benchmarks have on vendor selection: nobody looks behind the top level score!

This invites moral hazard when publishing a benchmark, and understandably shines a light on motivations and incentives at play, even if there are good intentions.  

As a consumer of models, if you are relying on benchmarks the least you should do is look at the traces from 3-5 failing tasks and try to make an informed decision yourself.  Vik has a checklist as well below.

Don't make up your mind based on twitter arguments either!  Look at the data.  Also sometimes "benchmarks of benchmarks" are slop.  You really need to look at the data yourself if you are making large purchasing decisions based on the numbers.

items.title: Modern software engineering increasingly relies on AI systems to autonomously resolve bug reports an...
items.content:
Modern software engineering increasingly relies on AI systems to autonomously resolve bug reports and issues. However, existing automated workflows face a major practical bottleneck when validating fixes: enterprise repositories contain massive regression test suites that take tens of minutes to execute, exceed model context windows, introduce noisy failures from flaky tests, and inflate operational costs. Conversely, running no regression tests risks deploying patches that break existing functionality. The article addresses this operational dilemma by introducing an automated technique, TestPrune, which identifies and executes only the small subset of existing regression tests directly relevant to a newly reported issue.

The main objective of the article is to formulate the issue-based test minimization problem—selecting tests relevant to an unknown, pending fix—and to evaluate how effectively TestPrune minimizes regression suites while enhancing automated bug reproduction and repair. The authors evaluated the approach across 800 real-world benchmark tasks from SWE-Bench Lite and SWE-Bench Verified using major frontier language models, including GPT-4o and Claude-3.7-Sonnet. TestPrune first prompts a model to locate suspicious functions and retrieve the ten most relevant test files, measures line-level execution coverage against those functions, and then executes a fast greedy algorithm to select a minimal test set that maximizes coverage of the potentially faulty code.

The J programming language is a highly terse, multi-paradigm array programming language developed in the early 1990s by Kenneth E. Iverson (the creator of APL) and Roger Hui. It is designed primarily for mathematical, statistical, and logical data analysis, making it exceptionally powerful for complex matrix computations and high-performance data processing.

This book introduces J through clear, worked examples that build from arithmetic to multidimensional arrays and function definitions, giving readers a practical path into its distinctive array-based style of programming.
